rationale: The BOOK ENTRY’s distinctive core (lost sheep = the already-scattered northern house of Israel mingled among the nations and thereafter sought/regathered) is not the best explanation of the supplied evidence. Matthew 15:24 is the sole verse printed with the entry; its narrative setting deploys the phrase precisely to refuse a Gentile petitioner and to contrast “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (children) with Gentiles (dogs). That contrast is fatal to an identification of the lost sheep as people already mixed into the nations. The same delimitation appears in the parallel mission charge of Matthew 10:5-6. The broader Lukan and Matthean lost-sheep parables (and the OT “sheep gone astray” texts) likewise portray ordinary sinners or straying Israelites, not a technical diaspora-Ephraim referent. The chapter’s synthesis of Hosea, Ezekiel’s sticks, and melo-ha-goyim supplies an interesting typological overlay, yet it cannot neutralize the plain mission-scope force of the very texts that employ the phrase. The secondary gloss (“any unrepentant sinner”) is uncontroversial but does not rescue the unsupported primary identification. The common reading therefore accounts for more of the decisive textual details with fewer unstated steps.
book_core_identification: The scattered house of Israel mingled with the nations, sought and regathered
unsupported_glossary_assertions: The scattered house of Israel mingled with the nations, sought and regathered (as the primary or definitional sense of “lost sheep”)
chapter_only_objections: Full two-house / Ephraim-as-seed-among-the-nations theology that equates the Gentile mission with the regathering of the lost tribes
Reading of the two olive trees / two sticks / two witnesses as the houses of Judah and Ephraim
Extension of Jacob’s name-change pattern into a comprehensive anthropology of every human heart that then becomes the lost-sheep referent
strongest_counter_interpretation: In ordinary NT usage the lost sheep is the sinner or spiritually straying person whom the divine Shepherd seeks and restores (Luke 15:3-7; Matt 18:12-14; cf. Isa 53:6; 1 Pet 2:25). The qualified phrase “lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt 10:6; 15:24) simply restricts Jesus’ and the apostles’ initial mission to the people of Israel as opposed to Gentiles or Samaritans; it does not encode a technical reference to the already-assimilated northern tribes now mingled among the nations.
counter_core_identification: Straying sinners (especially of Israel) whom God/Christ seeks, with Matt 15:24 marking the Israel-versus-Gentile scope of Jesus’ earthly mission
material_core_denial: The lost sheep of the house of Israel in the verse cited by the entry are not the scattered and already-mingled northern house; they are the contemporary people of Israel to whom Jesus declares Himself exclusively sent in explicit contrast to Gentiles.
counter_case: Matt 15:21-28 places the saying inside a refusal of a Canaanite woman and an Israel/Gentile (children/dogs) contrast; the lost sheep cannot therefore be people already counted among the nations.
Matt 10:5-6 pairs the identical phrase with an explicit ban on going to Gentiles or Samaritans, confirming mission-scope usage.
Luke 15:1-7 frames the parable as Jesus’ defense of receiving ordinary “sinners,” not as a program for retrieving the lost ten tribes.
The OT “sheep gone astray” texts (Isa 53:6; Ps 119:176; Ezek 34; Jer 50:6) speak of Israel’s or humanity’s general waywardness, not a post-exilic mingled remnant that has become the nations.
No supplied text requires or even suggests that “lost sheep” functions as a technical label for melo-ha-goyim / fullness-of-the-Gentiles.
book_explanatory_advantages: Links the phrase to Hosea’s “mixed himself among the people,” Ezekiel’s two sticks, and the melo-ha-goyim blessing on Ephraim
Offers a single Jacob–Israel–Ephraim narrative arc that can also underwrite the secondary “any sinner” sense
counter_explanatory_advantages: Preserves the explicit Israel-versus-Gentile contrast inside the only verse printed with the entry
Fits the narrative frames of both lost-sheep parables without remainder
Aligns with the overwhelming historic Christian consensus while still acknowledging the limited “house of Israel” mission texts
Requires no additional hypothesis that the Gentile mission is secretly the regathering of already-mingled Israelites
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: The immediate narrative of Matthew 15:21-28, in which “lost sheep of the house of Israel” is uttered to decline a Gentile request and to distinguish Israel from the nations
Matthew 10:5-6, which joins the same phrase to a prohibition against entering Gentile or Samaritan roads
unresolved_objections: The chapter’s broader typological connections (Ephraim’s scattering, two sticks, etc.) remain suggestive for other doctrines even if they do not control the glossary sense of “lost sheep”
